Gastroenterology · published research

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy

Summary of the Evidence

One open-label, single-centre randomized trial included 263 patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. It compared usual surgery with or without a single intraoperative red-LED exposure to the gallbladder bed and porta hepatis. The report focused on blood markers measured three days after surgery and did not establish a patient-centred recovery benefit (Redkin et al. 2017).

Human and clinical evidence

Postoperative increases in alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were smaller in the LED group than in controls. The randomized comparison supports a treatment-associated difference in these short-term laboratory outcomes. The accessible abstract reports statistical significance but gives no numerical between-group estimates or confidence intervals, and it does not establish less pain, fewer complications, a shorter hospital stay, or better longer-term recovery (Redkin et al. 2017).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly testing PBM during laparoscopic cholecystectomy was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial used a 625 ± 5-nm red LED with pulse-width modulation at 76 Hz and a 23% duty cycle. Reported irradiance was 15–30 mW/cm² and fluence was 0.9–1.8 J/cm². Light was delivered once for two minutes after gallbladder removal to the exposed operative bed and porta hepatis. This intraoperative route cannot be assumed to have the same effects as external treatment over intact skin. The study did not compare alternative wavelengths or doses (Redkin et al. 2017).

Interpretation

The randomized study found smaller short-term rises in three postoperative blood markers after red LED exposure. This is a favorable biomarker result, but does not by itself show that recovery was easier or complications were prevented. A blinded replication with patient-centred recovery measures would clarify whether the laboratory difference translates into a benefit for patients.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)Low for smaller short-term postoperative rises in ALT, AST, and ESRVery low for improved symptoms or fewer surgical complications

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One open-label randomized trial found a difference in short-term blood markers, but the published report does not establish a patient-centred recovery benefit. The biomarker findings come from a single study and lack a reported numerical between-group estimate in the accessible record. Replication with blinded assessment and outcomes such as pain, complications, and recovery would clarify their clinical relevance (Redkin et al. 2017).
